item.title: jscrambler npm Infostealer Compromise and Global CMS Exploitation Campaign
Encrypted PDF Sent via Authenticated Insurance Domain Evades Email Scanners

item.content:encoded:
Hackers Weaponize Balochistan Police Portal in Multi-Group Espionage Campaigns — Must Read

Suspected China- and India-aligned hackers compromised Pakistani law enforcement systems, including the Balochistan Police portal, to conduct espionage and deliver malware such as PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos RAT, and AsyncRAT. The campaign shows how high-value police platforms holding biometric, criminal, and citizen data can be turned into malware delivery infrastructure for both staff and the public.

  • Cybersecurity researchers reported sustained cyber espionage activity against Pakistani law enforcement organizations by suspected China- and India-aligned threat actors between February 2024 and April 2026.
  • The compromised Balochistan Police assets included servers hosting web applications that manage police and citizen data, such as criminal records, biometric records, hotel and tenant registrations, case files, and personnel records.
  • SentinelOne identified four threat clusters using PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, and Remcos RAT, with Remcos linked to an India-nexus actor and PlugX and ShadowPad traditionally associated with Chinese nation-state groups.
  • The Balochistan Police Complaint Management System was compromised to host implants named cms_plugin.exe, including a Rust stager and a .NET executable that loaded an AsyncRAT client.
  • SentinelOne also detected compromised infrastructure associated with the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Police, the Islamabad Police, and the Punjab Safe Cities Authority.

Australia warns of global campaign targeting vulnerable CMS platforms — Must Read

Australia’s Cyber Security Centre warned that attackers are globally scanning and exploiting vulnerable CMS platforms and plugins, including WordPress, Craft CMS, Joomla JCE, and others, to deploy webshells on compromised sites. Website admins should urgently patch CMS software, themes, and plugins, remove unused components, and monitor for unauthorized files or suspicious server processes.

  • The Australian Cyber Security Centre issued an alert about a global exploitation campaign targeting vulnerable content management systems and plugins.
  • The ACSC said many small- to medium-sized Australian businesses have been impacted, with webshells being deployed on their sites.
  • The campaign targets vulnerabilities in CMS platforms and plugins including WordPress, Craft CMS, MaxSite CMS, MetInfo CMS, and Joomla JCE.
  • The ACSC noted that the campaign might be supported by AI, which can help threat actors accelerate attacks and scale exploitation of emerging flaws.
  • Website administrators are advised to apply the latest security updates, remove unused components, enable automatic updates where possible, and monitor for unauthorized file creation.

Critical Zimbra Flaw Could Let Crafted Emails Run Malicious Code in User Sessions — Must Read

Zimbra is urging customers to update to version 10.1.19 to fix a critical stored XSS flaw in the Classic Web Client that could let crafted emails run malicious code when opened. Successful exploitation could expose mailbox data, session information, or account settings.

  • Zimbra is urging customers to apply updates for a critical stored cross-site scripting flaw affecting the Classic Web Client.
  • The flaw could let specially crafted emails execute malicious scripts in a user's session when the email is opened.
  • Zimbra said exploitation could allow access to mailbox information, session data, or account settings.
  • The vulnerability has not yet been assigned a CVE identifier, and Zimbra has not mentioned any in-the-wild exploitation.
  • Users are recommended to update to Zimbra Collaboration Suite version 10.1.19 for optimal protection.

Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install — Should Read

The compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm release ran a preinstall hook that dropped a cross-platform Rust infostealer targeting developer secrets, cloud credentials, wallets, sessions, and AI tool keys. Anyone who installed it should remove the version, check for persistence, and rotate all secrets the affected machine or CI environment could access.

  • The jscrambler npm package version 8.14.0 was compromised with a preinstall hook that drops and executes a native binary for Windows, macOS, or Linux during installation.
  • The malicious files dist/setup.js and dist/intro.js appeared in the published npm package but not in jscrambler's public source repository, whose latest tag remained 8.13.0.
  • Socket, StepSecurity, and SafeDep reported that the payload is a Rust infostealer targeting developer secrets including cloud credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, browser data, Bitwarden vaults, communications sessions, and AI coding tool configuration files.
  • The Linux payload can load an eBPF program into the kernel from memory, while the Windows and macOS builds include anti-debugging checks and persistence through a hidden scheduled task or LaunchAgent.
  • Users are advised to remove jscrambler@8.14.0 from lockfiles and caches, upgrade to 8.15.0 or pin to 8.13.0, investigate affected machines, rotate reachable secrets, and block the observed command-and-control IP addresses.

'Ghostcommit' hides prompt injection in images to fool AI agents, steal secrets — Should Read

Researchers demonstrated “Ghostcommit,” a prompt-injection attack that hides malicious instructions inside a PNG so AI code reviewers miss them, but coding agents later follow them and leak .env secrets encoded as harmless-looking numbers in source code. The key takeaway is that AI development tooling, not just the model, needs multimodal review and runtime controls to stop agents from reading and exfiltrating sensitive files.

  • Researchers at the University of Missouri-Kansas City’s ASSET Research Group built a proof-of-concept pull request called Ghostcommit that hides malicious instructions inside a PNG image.
  • The attack uses an AGENTS.md file that points an AI coding agent to the image, where the rendered text instructs it to read a repository’s .env file and encode its contents as integers in source code.
  • The article says CodeRabbit’s default configuration excludes image files from review and Bugbot returned no findings, allowing the malicious image-based prompt to pass review.
  • In one end-to-end run, Cursor driving Claude Sonnet emitted a 311-integer constant that decoded byte-for-byte to the entire .env file.
  • The researchers found that coding tools such as Cursor and Antigravity followed the image and leaked secrets under multiple models, while Anthropic’s Claude Code refused under every tested model.

The Encrypted PDF Your Scanner Trusts Is Hiding the Link It Cannot Read — Should Read

A phishing email sent through a real insurer’s authenticated Microsoft 365 mail infrastructure passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC, but hid malicious links inside an RC4-encrypted PDF that scanners could not inspect. The key lesson is that authenticated sender signals and clean static scans are not enough when encrypted attachments can conceal unreadable payloads.

  • An attacker delivered an encrypted PDF through a national insurance carrier's own authenticated mail infrastructure to an eligibility specialist at a state health and human services agency.
  • SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and ARC all passed under the brand's own reject policy, and Microsoft's composite authentication scored the message at 100.
  • The attached ten-page RC4-encrypted PDF contained five clickable link annotations with obfuscated, non-ASCII URI strings that static analysis could not resolve.
  • The email body supplied a callback phone number and email address that did not match the insurance carrier's primary published customer service line.
  • No automated engine flagged the message, and a human analyst quarantined it three days after delivery.
